'''Meers Oppenheim''' (born 1962, [[Bethesda, Maryland]]) is an American physicist who is Professor of [[Astronomy]] at [[Boston University]]. His primary research interests include computational and theoretical space plasma [[physics]], dynamics of the ionosphere and solar atmosphere, particle-wave interactions in [[plasma (physics)|plasmas]], and the physics of meteor trails.<ref name="Oppenheim BU Profile">{{cite web |title=Meers Oppenheim |url=http://www.bu.edu/csp/profiles/meers-oppenheim/ |website=BU Center for Space Physics |access-date=18 March 2021}}</ref>

==Education==
Oppenheim received his B.S. and M.Eng. in 1984 and 1990 from [[Cornell University]]'s School of Applied and Engineering Physics. He then received his Ph.D. of [[Electrical Engineering]] in 1995 from Cornell's Space Plasma Physics Group.<ref name="Oppenheim CV">{{cite web |title=Curriculum Vitae |url=http://www.bu.edu/csp/files/2018/08/Oppenheim-2018-CV.pdf |website=BU Center for Space Physics |access-date=18 March 2021}}</ref>

==Career==
Oppenheim began his career as a programmer and junior analyst at Jack Faucett Associates, Inc. in [[Chevy Chase, Maryland]] from 1980 to 1982.<ref name="Oppenheim CV" /> From 1984 to 1986, he worked as a staff physicist at the Physics International Corporation in [[San Leandro, California]].<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />

In 1988, Oppenheim was a research assistant at Cornell University. In 1995, he became a [[Max Planck Society]] Postdoctoral Scientist.<ref name="Oppenheim CV" /> In 1996, he became a research associate at the [[University of Colorado, Boulder]].<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />

In 1998, Oppenheim began working as an assistant professor of astronomy at [[Boston University]]. He became an associate professor in 2004, and in 2013, a full professor. In 2018, he became the director of graduate admissions at Boston University.<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />

==Scientific contributions==
Oppenheim studies space plasma physics using supercomputer simulations, theory, and data. He works on a range of research topics, including ionospheric and solar collisional plasmas, particle-wave interactions, and the physics of meteor trails. Since 2016, he has been working to incorporate the important effects of ionospheric turbulence into planetary scale simulations of the coupled magnetosphere, ionosphere and atmosphere. He has also been trying to model wave heating of the solar chromosphere. Most recently, he has also been working on understanding the effects of UV [[photoelectrons]] on the ionosphere and their observational consequences.<ref name="Oppenheim BU Profile" />

* 1996: National Research Council Fellowship<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2001: Elected member, Union Radio Science International<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2002–2005: Elected Vice-Chair, Union Radio Science International<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2003–2005: Member, American Physical Science, Division of Plasma Physics, program committee<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2006–present: Elected Chair, Union Radio Science International, U.S.A. Commission H<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2008–2011: Elected member, CEDAR Science Steering Committee<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2011–2014: Elected Vice-Chair, Union Radio Science International, International Commission H<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2016: CEDAR Prize Lecturer<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* 2018: Visiting Scholar and Professor, Leibniz-Institut f ̈ur Atmosph ̈arenphysik, Kuhlungsborn, Germany<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* Member of the [[American Geophysical Union]]<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* Member of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
* Member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref name="Oppenheim CV" />
